definition: The factored language model (FLM) is an extension of a conventional language model introduced by Jeff Bilmes and Katrin Kirchoff in 2003.
details: In an FLM, each word is viewed as a vector of k factors: w i = { f i 1 , . . . , f i k } . {\displaystyle w_{i}=\{f_{i}^{1},...,f_{i}^{k}\}.} An FLM provides the probabilistic model P ( f | f 1 , . . . , f N ) {\displaystyle P(f|f_{1},...,f_{N})} where the prediction of a factor f {\displaystyle f} is based on N {\displaystyle N} parents { f 1 , . . . , f N } {\displaystyle \{f_{1},...,f_{N}\}} . For example, if w {\displaystyle w} represents a word token and t {\displaystyle t} represents a Part of speech tag for English, the expression P ( w i | w i − 2 , w i − 1 , t i − 1 ) {\displaystyle P(w_{i}|w_{i-2},w_{i-1},t_{i-1})} gives a model for predicting current word token based on a traditional Ngram model as well as the Part of speech tag of the previous word. A major advantage of factored language models is that they allow users to specify linguistic knowledge such as the relationship between word tokens and Part of speech in English, or morphological information (stems, root, etc.) in Arabic. Like N-gram models, smoothing techniques are necessary in parameter estimation. In particular, generalized back-off is used in training an FLM.

explainer.lead: A factored language model predicts words using several kinds of information about each word, rather than treating every word as a single indivisible token. This lets it incorporate linguistic clues such as part-of-speech tags or morphological structure alongside earlier words.

tiers.eli5: Imagine each word comes with several labels, like its spelling, its grammatical job, and its root. To guess what comes next, this model can look at earlier words and some of those labels, giving it more useful clues than earlier words alone.
tiers.practitioner: To apply an FLM, represent each word as a vector of factors and select which earlier factors should condition the target. For example, an English model can combine the previous two tokens with the previous part-of-speech tag. Parameter estimation still requires smoothing, specifically generalized back-off, as with n-gram models.
tiers.paperLevel: Each word is represented as w_i = {f_i^1, ..., f_i^k}, and the model estimates P(f | f_1, ..., f_N), where f is a target factor and its N parents are selected conditioning factors. Introduced by Jeff Bilmes and Katrin Kirchoff in 2003, it extends conventional language modeling with linguistic factors but still requires smoothing during parameter estimation, using generalized back-off.

explainer.example: In English, P(w_i | w_{i-2}, w_{i-1}, t_{i-1}) predicts the current word token from the previous two word tokens and the previous word's part-of-speech tag t. Thus the context combines an ordinary n-gram-style word history with grammatical information.

usedIn.name: English language modeling
usedIn.detail: Combines word-token history with part-of-speech information to predict the current word.

usedIn.name: Arabic language modeling
usedIn.detail: Incorporates morphological information such as stems and roots into word prediction.

components.name: Factor vectors
components.detail: Represent each word as k factors rather than a single token.

components.name: Parent factors
components.detail: A selected set of N earlier factors supplies the conditioning context.

components.name: Conditional model
components.detail: Estimates the probability of a target factor given its parent factors.

components.name: Generalized back-off
components.detail: Provides the smoothing used when estimating model parameters.

flow: Represent each word as a vector of linguistic factors.
Select N parent factors as the prediction context.
Estimate the target factor's conditional probability using generalized back-off during training.
Use the resulting distribution to predict the target factor.
explainer.origin: Jeff Bilmes and Katrin Kirchoff introduced the factored language model in 2003 as an extension of conventional language modeling.
explainer.lineage: FLMs retain the conditional-history approach of n-gram models while adding linguistic structure such as part-of-speech and morphology. Like n-gram models, they depend on smoothing, with generalized back-off used for training.
explainer.whyItMatters: The model gives language modelers a direct way to encode relationships between words and linguistic annotations. That can make prediction context richer than a sequence of word tokens alone.
